● Margin and measurement

Contribution margin and the ROAS you need to break even.

A ROAS can look healthy and still lose money. Here is how to work out what an order really leaves behind, and the ROAS you need to break even.

Break-even ROAS calculator
  • 4 min read
  • By Monday Marketing Company
  1. Home
  2. Insights
  3. Margin and measurement
In this guide
  1. What contribution margin is
  2. Why revenue and platform ROAS mislead
  3. How to work it out, step by step
  4. A worked example
  5. Why returns and failed deliveries change the answer
  6. How to use break-even ROAS
  7. Work it out with your own numbers
Jump to the questionsAll insights

In short

Contribution margin is what is left of an order's revenue after the costs that come with that order, and break-even ROAS is the ROAS at which ad spend uses up exactly that amount.

  • Start from one orderWhat it earns, and what it costs to deliver.
  • One simple formulaBreak-even ROAS is 1 divided by contribution margin.
  • Then compareSet it against the ROAS the platform reports.

What contribution margin is

Contribution margin is the money an order leaves behind after the costs that vary with that order. For a D2C brand these are product cost, packaging, shipping, payment gateway fees and the cost of returns. Rent, salaries and software are fixed costs and sit outside it.

It matters because it is the pool your advertising has to be paid from. Whatever an order leaves behind before ads is the most you can spend to win that order and still break even.

The short versionContribution margin before ads, as a share of revenue, sets your break-even ROAS. Break-even ROAS is 1 divided by that share.

Why revenue and platform ROAS mislead

ROAS divides the revenue an ad platform reports by what you spent on ads. It says nothing about what it cost to make and deliver those orders. Two brands can both report the same ROAS and one can be profitable while the other loses money on every sale.

Also check whether the revenue in your ROAS includes tax. Compare like with like: use the same basis for the ROAS you read and the margin you calculate.

How to work it out, step by step

  1. Start with the order valueUse the average order value, before tax if your costs are before tax.
  2. Subtract product costWhat it costs you to buy or make the items in that order.
  3. Subtract packaging and shippingInclude the forward shipping you pay, and cash-on-delivery handling if you offer it.
  4. Subtract payment feesGateway and collection charges on the order.
  5. Subtract a returns allowanceThe average cost of returns and failed deliveries, spread across all orders.
  6. Divide what is left by the order valueThat is your contribution margin before ads. Divide 1 by it to get break-even ROAS.
Free toolBreak-even ROAS calculatorTry it: enter your own costs and see your break-even ROAS.

A worked example

The numbers below are made up to show the method. Use your own.

LinePer order (₹)Share of order value
Order value (before tax)1,000100%
Product cost30030%
Packaging404%
Shipping909%
Payment fees202%
Returns allowance505%
Contribution before ads50050%

Illustrative example, not a benchmark

What that givesContribution before ads is 50% of order value, so break-even ROAS is 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.0. Break-even cost per order is ₹500. A campaign at ROAS 3.0 leaves margin after ads. A campaign at ROAS 1.8 loses money even though it looks healthy.

Why returns and failed deliveries change the answer

A returned or refused order earns nothing but still costs shipping, often both ways, plus packaging and handling. For brands that ship cash on delivery, this can move break-even ROAS by a full point or more.

That is why the returns allowance is its own line. If you do not include it, your break-even ROAS looks lower than it really is, and campaigns look safer than they are.

How to use break-even ROAS

  • Set a floor: campaigns below break-even ROAS need a fix or a pause, unless they are bringing customers who reorder.
  • Set a target above it: the gap between your ROAS and break-even is the margin your ads leave.
  • Change it when your costs change: a price rise, a cheaper courier or lower returns all move break-even ROAS.
  • Read repeat customers separately. A first order that only breaks even can still pay off if the customer comes back. See the LTV:CAC calculator.

Common questions

Questions people ask about contribution margin and break-even ROAS.

What is contribution margin?
It is the money left from an order after the costs that vary with it: product, packaging, shipping, payment fees and returns. It is the pool your ads are paid from.
How do you calculate break-even ROAS?
Divide 1 by your contribution margin before ads, as a share of order value. If the margin is 50%, break-even ROAS is 2.0.
Is a ROAS of 3 good?
It depends on your margin. If break-even ROAS is 2, a ROAS of 3 leaves margin. If break-even is 3.5, the same ROAS loses money.
Should the ROAS include tax?
Compare like with like. Use the same tax basis for the ROAS you read and the margin you calculate.
Where can I calculate mine?
Use the break-even ROAS calculator with your own costs.
